results.name: two_example_interpolation_vs_extrapolation
results.description: In two-example sets whose examples are >= 6 apart, yes rate for non-example targets strictly between them minus yes rate for targets outside their range but within one gap-length of the nearer example; observed > null means people interpolate between examples more sharply than they extrapolate beyond them, beyond what the model's interval hypotheses produce; observed < null means extrapolation is stronger than modelled.
results.code:
# name: two_example_interpolation_vs_extrapolation
# description: In two-example sets whose examples are >= 6 apart, yes rate for non-example targets strictly between them minus yes rate for targets outside their range but within one gap-length of the nearer example; observed > null means people interpolate between examples more sharply than they extrapolate beyond them, beyond what the model's interval hypotheses produce; observed < null means extrapolation is stronger than modelled.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    valid = ~np.isnan(ex)
    n = valid.sum(axis=1)
    dist = np.where(valid, np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), np.inf)
    d = dist.min(axis=1)
    lo = np.where(valid, ex, np.inf).min(axis=1)
    hi = np.where(valid, ex, -np.inf).max(axis=1)
    gap = hi - lo
    base = (n == 2) & (gap >= 6) & (d > 0)
    a = base & (t > lo) & (t < hi)
    b = base & ((t < lo) | (t > hi)) & (d <= gap)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(y[a].mean() - y[b].mean())

results.name: outlier_beyond_radius_yes
results.description: In sets of >= 3 examples with exactly one minority-parity example, yes rate for minority-parity non-example targets 4-9 away from that outlier and more than 3 from every majority example; observed > null means the outlier's exception region extends farther than the model's (radius <= 3) neighbourhood, observed < null means it is narrower.
results.code:
# name: outlier_beyond_radius_yes
# description: In sets of >= 3 examples with exactly one minority-parity example, yes rate for minority-parity non-example targets 4-9 away from that outlier and more than 3 from every majority example; observed > null means the outlier's exception region extends farther than the model's (radius <= 3) neighbourhood, observed < null means it is narrower.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    valid = ~np.isnan(ex)
    n = valid.sum(axis=1)
    dist = np.where(valid, np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), np.inf)
    d = dist.min(axis=1)
    par = np.where(valid, np.mod(ex, 2), -1)
    odd = (par == 1).sum(axis=1)
    even = (par == 0).sum(axis=1)
    one_out = (n >= 3) & ((odd == 1) | (even == 1)) & (odd != even)
    minp = np.where(odd == 1, 1, 0)
    is_out = par == minp[:, None]
    d_out = np.where(is_out, dist, np.inf).min(axis=1)
    d_maj = np.where(~is_out & valid, dist, np.inf).min(axis=1)
    m = one_out & (d > 0) & (d_out >= 4) & (d_out <= 9) & (d_maj > 3) & (np.mod(t, 2) == minp)
    return float(y[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0

results.name: partial_final_digit_far_same_parity
results.description: In sets of >= 2 examples sharing one parity but not all ending in the same digit, among same-parity non-example targets >= 5 from every example, yes rate when the target's final digit matches some example's final digit minus when it matches none; observed > null means people generalize by partial final-digit resemblance that no single rule in the model captures, observed < null means less than modelled.
results.code:
# name: partial_final_digit_far_same_parity
# description: In sets of >= 2 examples sharing one parity but not all ending in the same digit, among same-parity non-example targets >= 5 from every example, yes rate when the target's final digit matches some example's final digit minus when it matches none; observed > null means people generalize by partial final-digit resemblance that no single rule in the model captures, observed < null means less than modelled.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    valid = ~np.isnan(ex)
    n = valid.sum(axis=1)
    dist = np.where(valid, np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), np.inf)
    d = dist.min(axis=1)
    par = np.where(valid, np.mod(ex, 2), -1)
    odd = (par == 1).sum(axis=1)
    even = (par == 0).sum(axis=1)
    uni = (n >= 2) & ((odd == n) | (even == n))
    setp = np.where(odd == n, 1, 0)
    fd = np.where(valid, np.mod(ex, 10), -1)
    fdmax = fd.max(axis=1)
    fdmin = np.where(valid, fd, 99).min(axis=1)
    mixed = fdmax != fdmin
    share = (fd == np.mod(t, 10)[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    base = uni & mixed & (np.mod(t, 2) == setp) & (d >= 5)
    a, b = base & share, base & ~share
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(y[a].mean() - y[b].mean())

results.name: uniform_parity_inrange_opposite_yes
results.description: In sets of >= 3 examples that all share one parity, yes rate for opposite-parity targets lying strictly between the smallest and largest example; observed > null means people let the examples' range (similarity) override the parity rule more than modelled, observed < null means they apply the parity rule more strictly than modelled.

results.name: outlier_example_self_yes
results.description: In sets of >= 3 examples with exactly one minority-parity example, yes rate when the target is that outlier example itself; observed < null means people reject the anomalous example (treat it as noise) more than the model's exception concepts predict, observed > null means they accept it more.
results.code:
# name: outlier_example_self_yes
# description: In sets of >= 3 examples with exactly one minority-parity example, yes rate when the target is that outlier example itself; observed < null means people reject the anomalous example (treat it as noise) more than the model's exception concepts predict, observed > null means they accept it more.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    valid = ~np.isnan(ex)
    n = valid.sum(axis=1)
    dist = np.where(valid, np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), np.inf)
    d = dist.min(axis=1)
    par = np.where(valid, np.mod(ex, 2), -1)
    odd = (par == 1).sum(axis=1)
    even = (par == 0).sum(axis=1)
    one_out = (n >= 3) & ((odd == 1) | (even == 1)) & (odd != even)
    minp = np.where(odd == 1, 1, 0)
    is_out = par == minp[:, None]
    hit = (is_out & (ex == t[:, None])).any(axis=1)
    m = one_out & hit
    return float(y[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0

results.name: math_rule_far_member_yes
results.description: In sets of >= 2 examples that are all powers of 2, all perfect squares, or all perfect cubes, yes rate for non-example targets belonging to that same mathematical family and >= 5 from every example; observed > null means people extend mathematical rules to distant members more than modelled, observed < null means they prefer range/similarity over the math rule more than modelled.
results.code:
# name: math_rule_far_member_yes
# description: In sets of >= 2 examples that are all powers of 2, all perfect squares, or all perfect cubes, yes rate for non-example targets belonging to that same mathematical family and >= 5 from every example; observed > null means people extend mathematical rules to distant members more than modelled, observed < null means they prefer range/similarity over the math rule more than modelled.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    valid = ~np.isnan(ex)
    n = valid.sum(axis=1)
    dist = np.where(valid, np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), np.inf)
    d = dist.min(axis=1)
    fams = [np.array([2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64]), np.array([k * k for k in range(1, 11)]), np.array([1, 8, 27, 64])]
    m = np.zeros(len(t), dtype=bool)
    for f in fams:
        allin = (np.isin(ex, f) | ~valid).all(axis=1) & (n >= 2)
        m |= allin & np.isin(t, f) & (d >= 5)
    return float(y[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0

results.name: decade_boundary_contrast
results.description: For non-example targets 1-6 away from their nearest example, the distance-stratified (count-weighted) yes rate when the target shares the nearest example's tens digit minus when it is across a decade boundary; observed > null means people treat decades ("the 20s") as categories that the model's smooth intervals/neighbourhoods under-produce, observed < null means the model over-produces a decade effect.
results.code:
# name: decade_boundary_contrast
# description: For non-example targets 1-6 away from their nearest example, the distance-stratified (count-weighted) yes rate when the target shares the nearest example's tens digit minus when it is across a decade boundary; observed > null means people treat decades ("the 20s") as categories that the model's smooth intervals/neighbourhoods under-produce, observed < null means the model over-produces a decade effect.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    valid = ~np.isnan(ex)
    n = valid.sum(axis=1)
    dist = np.where(valid, np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), np.inf)
    d = dist.min(axis=1)
    nearest = np.take_along_axis(np.where(valid, ex, np.nan), np.argmin(dist, axis=1)[:, None], axis=1)[:, 0]
    same = np.floor(nearest / 10) == np.floor(t / 10)
    tot, wsum = 0.0, 0.0
    for k in range(1, 7):
        m = d == k
        a, b = m & same, m & ~same
        if a.sum() > 0 and b.sum() > 0:
            w = float(m.sum())
            tot += w * (y[a].mean() - y[b].mean())
            wsum += w
    return float(tot / wsum) if wsum > 0 else 0.0

results.name: digit_rule_set_offdigit_neighbour_yes
results.description: In sets of >= 3 examples that all end in the same digit, yes rate for targets with a different final digit lying 1-3 from some example; observed > null means people keep similarity-based (neighbour) generalization even when a sharp final-digit rule fits, more than modelled; observed < null means the digit rule suppresses neighbours more than modelled.
results.code:
# name: digit_rule_set_offdigit_neighbour_yes
# description: In sets of >= 3 examples that all end in the same digit, yes rate for targets with a different final digit lying 1-3 from some example; observed > null means people keep similarity-based (neighbour) generalization even when a sharp final-digit rule fits, more than modelled; observed < null means the digit rule suppresses neighbours more than modelled.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    valid = ~np.isnan(ex)
    n = valid.sum(axis=1)
    dist = np.where(valid, np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), np.inf)
    d = dist.min(axis=1)
    fd = np.where(valid, np.mod(ex, 10), -1)
    fdmax = fd.max(axis=1)
    fdmin = np.where(valid, fd, 99).min(axis=1)
    same = (n >= 3) & (fdmax == fdmin)
    m = same & (np.mod(t, 10) != fdmax) & (d >= 1) & (d <= 3)
    return float(y[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0
